stimulus.title: Why Do Leaves Change Colour?
stimulus.body: Every autumn, forests across southern Australia put on a quiet but spectacular display as certain deciduous trees shift from green to gold, orange and deep red. Once the green pigment fades, other pigments that were present all along, but masked by the abundant chlorophyll, finally become visible. Some trees also produce brand new red pigments at this time, possibly as a defence against sunlight damage while the tree withdraws its remaining nutrients.

Because the tree is attracting insects to help spread its seeds before winter.

stimulus.title: The Beekeeper's Warning
stimulus.body: Nadia had visited her grandfather's orchard every summer since she could walk, but she had never been allowed near the beehives until this year. 'Bees are not our enemies,' her grandfather said, tightening the strap on her borrowed veil, 'but they are diplomats, not pushovers. Move like a shadow, and they will forgive almost anything.' Nadia laughed nervously, though her stomach had turned into a nest of hornets itself. As they approached the first hive, she noticed her grandfather's steps slow to an almost theatrical crawl, his breathing low and even. options.text: It suggests her nervousness felt sharp, buzzing and slightly dangerous, echoing the bees she was about to face.
It shows that Nadia had accidentally disturbed a real nest of hornets earlier that day.
It proves that Nadia was more frightened of hornets than of bees.
It explains why her grandfather decided she was not ready to visit the hives.

questions.explanation: The comparison to a 'nest of hornets' is figurative, not literal, since nothing in the text suggests a real hornet encounter. A plainer word such as 'nervous' would have described her feeling accurately, but would not have connected it to the world of stinging insects she is about to enter. Choosing hornets instead lets the author echo the danger and buzz of the bees themselves, making Nadia's anxiety feel sharper and more physical. stimulus.body: Every autumn, forests across southern Australia put on a quiet but spectacular display as certain deciduous trees shift from green to gold, orange and deep red. As daylight shortens, trees begin to reabsorb chlorophyll from their leaves, effectively recycling a valuable resource before the leaves are shed. Once the green pigment fades, other pigments that were present all along, but masked by the abundant chlorophyll, finally become visible. Some trees also produce brand new red pigments at this time, possibly as a defence against sunlight damage while the tree withdraws its remaining nutrients.

options.text: To take a substance back into the plant after it had been held elsewhere in the leaf.
To release a substance permanently into the surrounding air.
To destroy a substance completely so it can never be used again.
To photograph or record a substance for later scientific study.

The prefix 're-' combined with 'absorb' also suggests taking something back in, rather than sending it outward. Considering the prefix, the surrounding words, and the recycling context together confirms that 'reabsorb' means taking the substance back into the plant for reuse.

The phrase also rules out the idea of bees being weak or unreactive, since a 'pushover' is exactly that kind of easily-overcome creature, and the grandfather is denying that description. Equally, calling them diplomats rather than simply dangerous suggests they are not aggressive without reason, but capable of being reasoned with under the right conditions.

questions.prompt: In the passage, what does the word 'deciduous' most likely describe?

stimulus.title: Why Do Leaves Change Colour?
stimulus.body: Every autumn, forests across southern Australia put on a quiet but spectacular display as certain deciduous trees shift from green to gold, orange and deep red. The transformation is not caused by cooling temperatures alone, but by a gradual reduction in daylight hours, which signals to the tree that winter is approaching. Throughout spring and summer, leaves are dominated by chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight and gives leaves their familiar green colour. As daylight shortens, trees begin to reabsorb chlorophyll from their leaves, effectively recycling a valuable resource before the leaves are shed. Once the green pigment fades, other pigments that were present all along, but masked by the abundant chlorophyll, finally become visible. Some trees also produce brand new red pigments at this time, possibly as a defence against sunlight damage while the tree withdraws its remaining nutrients.

options.text: Trees that lose their leaves at a particular time of year.
Trees that keep exactly the same leaves all year round.
Trees that only grow in very cold climates.
Trees that never produce flowers or fruit.

questions.explanation: The passage describes 'certain deciduous trees' changing colour 'before the leaves are shed,' directly linking the word to trees that lose their leaves. The phrase 'before the leaves are shed' is the key context clue, since 'shed' means to drop or lose something. This rules out trees that keep the same leaves all year, since shedding leaves is the opposite of that idea. Nothing in the passage links 'deciduous' to a particular climate or to a lack of flowers, so those options can be ruled out too.

questions.prompt: What can readers infer about Nadia's experience with beehives before the events of this passage?

stimulus.title: The Beekeeper's Warning
stimulus.body: Nadia had visited her grandfather's orchard every summer since she could walk, but she had never been allowed near the beehives until this year. 'Bees are not our enemies,' her grandfather said, tightening the strap on her borrowed veil, 'but they are diplomats, not pushovers. Move like a shadow, and they will forgive almost anything.' Nadia laughed nervously, though her stomach had turned into a nest of hornets itself. As they approached the first hive, she noticed her grandfather's steps slow to an almost theatrical crawl, his breathing low and even. A single bee landed on her sleeve and simply sat there, as if deciding whether she was worth the trouble of a sting. Nadia held perfectly still, remembering his warning, and after a long moment the bee lifted off and drifted back towards the hive entrance without incident.

options.text: She had never been close to the hives before this visit.
She had helped her grandfather manage the hives for many years.
She was more experienced with bees than her grandfather was.
She had been stung by bees several times in the past.

questions.explanation: The passage states directly that Nadia 'had never been allowed near the beehives until this year,' which tells readers she lacked prior close experience with them. This is true even though she had visited the orchard itself for many summers, since visiting an orchard is not the same as being allowed near its hives. Nothing in the passage suggests she had helped manage the hives, been stung previously, or was more experienced than her grandfather. Only the first option is directly supported by the passage's own wording about this being her first time near the hives.

questions.prompt: Maria completely and carelessly forgot to pack her favourite umbrella before hurriedly leaving for school that particular drizzly morning; ___, she was thoroughly soaked from head to toe by the time she finally reached the crowded, sheltered bus stop. Complete the blank with the connective that best shows a cause-and-effect relationship.

segments: Maria forgot her umbrella;
, she was soaked by the time she reached the bus stop.

questions.explanation: Forgetting the umbrella is the direct cause of Maria getting soaked on her way to school, so a cause-and-effect connective is required here. Words such as 'as a result', 'consequently', 'therefore' or 'so' correctly link the two clauses, showing that the second event follows logically from the first. A contrast connective such as 'however' would not make sense here, since nothing in the sentence suggests an unexpected or opposing outcome. An addition connective such as 'also' would likewise fail to capture the causal relationship the sentence describes.
